findings.claim: CHANGES.md asserts this is a pure refactor where 'every column kind that used to be picked up by the alias-list call is still picked up here, and nothing else is,' and the module docstring lists three text-like aliases ('text', 'masked_text', 'choice'). But the bundled test suite never constructs or asserts on a 'masked_text' column, so the parity claim for that specific alias is unverified by any test in this pack.
findings.source: columnstore.py:64 `return kind in {"text", "masked_text", "choice"}`; test_columnstore.py:17-31 `_table()`/`test_encodes_text_and_choice_including_packed` construct and assert only "text", "number", "choice", and their Packed variants -- no "masked_text" column exists in the fixture
findings.remedy: Add a `masked_text` (and `Packed("masked_text")`) column to the `_table()` fixture and assert it appears in `encode_categoricals`'s result, so the behavior-parity claim in CHANGES.md is actually covered.

findings.claim: `column_subset` and `should_encode` each independently repeat the identical Packed-unwrap ternary. Nothing about the two call sites depends on that unwrap logic differing -- only the alias set / return shape differs -- so the duplication is a real, if small, drift risk (e.g. a future Packed-like wrapper is unwrapped correctly in one place and forgotten in the other).
findings.source: columnstore.py:53 `alias = col.kind.primitive if isinstance(col.kind, Packed) else col.kind` and columnstore.py:63 `kind = col.kind.primitive if isinstance(col.kind, Packed) else col.kind`
findings.remedy: Factor the unwrap into a small private helper, e.g. `def _primitive(kind: str | Packed) -> str`, and call it from both `column_subset` and `should_encode`. No caller-visible change.

findings.claim: `_DERIVED_PATTERN` was written to also match a `Tagged[...]`-prefixed unresolved forward reference (the optional `((\w+\.)?Tagged\[)?` group), and that branch is reachable through `is_derived_annotation`'s fallback when a Tagged-wrapped annotation fails to eval. But no test exercises that combination -- the only Tagged test (`test_tagged_wrapped_derived_field_is_excluded`) uses `Tagged[Derived[int], "cache"]`, which resolves successfully and never reaches the regex fallback at all.
findings.source: fieldspec.py:24 `_DERIVED_PATTERN = re.compile(r"((\w+\.)?Tagged\[)?(\w+\.)?Derived\[")`; test_fieldspec.py:37-41 `test_tagged_wrapped_derived_field_is_excluded` only covers the fully-resolvable case
findings.remedy: Add a case like `stored_field_names({"total": "int", "cached_total": 'Tagged[Derived[Missing], "cache"]'}, NAMESPACE)` (where `Missing` is absent from `NAMESPACE`) to prove the Tagged-prefixed regex fallback actually excludes the field, not just the bare-Derived fallback.

findings.claim: `Handle.span` was narrowed from what CHANGES.md implies was a plain writable `str` attribute to a read-only property with no setter. CHANGES.md's compatibility guarantee is explicitly scoped to readers ('Every existing caller that only ever read `.span` sees no change'), and the test suite only ever reads `.span` (equality, dict-key, formatting) -- it never assigns to it. If any existing caller previously did `handle.span = ...`, that call now raises `AttributeError: can't set attribute`, and nothing here proves that no such caller exists.
findings.source: lifespan.py:70-72 `@property\n    def span(self) -> str:\n        return self._span.value` (no setter defined); CHANGES.md:9 "Every existing caller that only ever read `.span` sees no change."
findings.remedy: Either add a setter (`@span.setter def span(self, value: str): self._span = Span(value)`) to preserve write-through compatibility, or grep the consuming codebase for `.span =` assignments and record that none exist as the executable evidence this claim needs.

findings.claim: `Span.__lt__` rebuilds `list(self.__class__)` on every comparison, duplicating the module-level `SPANS = list(Span)` that already exists for exactly this purpose. Nothing depends on the two lists differing.
findings.source: lifespan.py:32 `order = list(self.__class__)` inside `__lt__`, vs. lifespan.py:36 `SPANS = list(Span)`
findings.remedy: Have `__lt__` use the module-level `SPANS` constant instead of rebuilding the list locally.

findings.claim: `actor QuietQueue {}` is defined but never referenced by `Workspace`, `child(_:at:)`, or anything in main.swift. It is speculative scaffolding for a feature that doesn't exist yet. The deletion test passes cleanly: removing it changes nothing for any caller in either file.
findings.source: workspace.swift:57-59 `// Reserved for a future default execution context; not wired into any\n// scoping path yet.\nactor QuietQueue {}`
findings.remedy: Delete `QuietQueue`. If a default execution context is genuinely planned, add it when a caller actually needs it -- an unwired actor sitting in the same file as the type it will supposedly serve invites someone to assume it's already load-bearing.

findings.claim: CHANGES.md's central behavior-preservation claim for this refactor is 'No test's skip/run outcome changes on any platform' -- but `main()` in the bundled test suite only ever calls `collect_skips` with `MAINLAND`, the one platform where nothing is guarded and the assertion is simply `skipped == {}`. Neither `GEARSHIFT` nor `TIDELINE` -- the two platforms `is_driftplane` actually consolidates, and the only platforms where any guard (single- or double-stacked) fires -- is ever passed to `collect_skips` anywhere in this file. The refactor's one stated guarantee is therefore asserted but not exercised by the suite that ships with it.
findings.source: test_platform_guards.py:74-79 `def main() -> int:\n    skipped = collect_skips(MAINLAND, ALL_TESTS)\n    assert skipped == {}, ...` (only call to `collect_skips` in the file); CHANGES.md:11-12 "No test's skip/run outcome changes on any platform."
findings.remedy: Extend `main()` (or add a small helper) to call `collect_skips(GEARSHIFT, ALL_TESTS)` and `collect_skips(TIDELINE, ALL_TESTS)` and assert the expected skip sets on each -- including the three `is_driftplane`-consolidated tests and the two double-guard tests -- so the consolidation's behavior parity is actually demonstrated, not just narrated.
